name: Pathayam — the Kerala Granary Chest
tagline: The great wooden grain chest of the Kerala tharavad
summary: Pathayam, the traditional wooden granary of Kerala tharavads: how it was built, why it mattered, and where to see one in a heritage home.
description: A pathayam is a large, tightly joined wooden chest or room-sized box used to store paddy and other grain in traditional Kerala houses. It was usually built from jackfruit or teak, raised on feet and fitted with a small opening, to keep out damp, rodents and insects.
Pathayams of rice stood inside the tharavad (ancestral house) or in a detached store, and a family's wealth was often counted in the paddy stored there.

history.significance: A symbol of food security and family prosperity in the agrarian, matrilineal tharavad households that shaped Kerala society.

timeline.event: Paddy farming and the joint-family tharavad system make large grain stores a feature of well-to-do homes.
Carpenter families produce fine, carved pathayams as part of nalukettu construction.
Land reform, nuclear families and modern storage reduce use; pathayams survive in heritage homes and museums.

keyFacts: A pathayam could hold many hundreds of kilograms of paddy.
Paddy was measured in traditional units such as para and edangazhi.
The carpenter's skill is in the joinery: tight fitting with little or no metal.
Smaller pathayam-style chests are sold today as storage furniture.

folklore.title: The Granary and the Goddess
story: Households speak of the granary as the seat of Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and grain. At harvest the first sheaves and the first filling of the pathayam are marked with prayer and a lamp.
Another widespread custom is to keep a measure of paddy untouched in the pathayam as a promise of continued plenty.
folklore.note: Practices vary between communities and families; this is a general account.

spiritual.summary: The pathayam recalls a way of life based on harvest, sharing and thrift.

experiences.title: See one in a tharavad
experiences.text: Ask your host or museum guide to open a pathayam and explain how it was filled and measured.

experiences.title: Join a harvest event
experiences.text: In Kuttanad and Palakkad, harvest time offers a chance to see how grain reaches the granary.

mindfulTips: Do not climb on or sit on antique chests.

highlights: Joinery without nails in jackwood and teak
Linked to Lakshmi and harvest customs

visitorInfo.bestTime: Harvest months: September–October and January–February in much of Kerala.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Seen in nalukettu homes, folk museums and palace museums in Thiruvananthapuram, Ernakulam and Palakkad.
etiquette: Do not touch exhibits in museums.

whereToSee.name: Kerala Folklore Museum, Thripunithura
whereToSee.note: Private museum housed in a building assembled from traditional timber architecture; displays household objects, lamps and ritual items.

whereToSee.name: Koyikkal Palace Museum, Nedumangad
whereToSee.note: Nalukettu-style palace with a folklore and numismatics museum run by the State Archaeology Department.

whereToSee.name: Padmanabhapuram Palace
whereToSee.district: Kanniyakumari (Tamil Nadu), managed by Kerala Archaeology
whereToSee.note: Timber palace of the Travancore kings with carved ceilings; a short drive across the Kerala border from Thiruvananthapuram.

whereToBuy.name: Surabhi — Handicrafts Development Corporation of Kerala emporiums
whereToBuy.note: State-run emporiums selling metalcraft, wood carving, coir and handloom; good for fixed-price first purchases.

whereToBuy.name: Master carpenters in Thrissur and Palakkad
whereToBuy.note: Commission small pathayam-style chests from traditional carpenters; ask for references.

experiences.name: Kuthiramalika (Puthenmalika) Palace Museum
experiences.note: Travancore palace with carved horse brackets, in the Padmanabhaswamy Temple precinct.

experiences.name: Hill Palace Museum, Tripunithura
experiences.note: Former Cochin royal residence set in a hill-top campus with a museum of royal artefacts.

buyingTips: Antique pathayams may need an export permit; ask the seller about Archaeological Survey rules for objects over 100 years old.
New pieces should be solid wood, with visible joinery.
